pages.editorial_addition:
## Original decision model — a finite worker and waiting budget

Consider a fictional endpoint with four workers and room for eight waiting tasks. At an instant when all twelve slots are occupied, another attempt needs an explicit outcome: reject it, wait within a caller-owned budget, or defer it through a separately durable protocol. Merely calling the endpoint asynchronous does not answer that question. These numbers describe an invented state, not a Java default or a measured safe configuration.

Now let the downstream dependency pause. The relevant inventory includes active tasks waiting downstream, accepted tasks waiting locally, their remaining deadlines and work already committed beyond the process. A larger waiting queue postpones a capacity decision and retains more state; it does not make the dependency complete operations faster. If tasks continue after the callers abandon them, the system can consume scarce capacity on results nobody can use.

Before changing the pool, write the required behavior for a saturated queue, an expired caller, a failed worker and process shutdown. For each accepted operation, identify whether it is safe to discard, retry with the same logical identity, or query an authoritative outcome. Compare a smaller bounded pool plus explicit admission with a larger pool under the same offered workload and downstream permits. The discriminating result is correct completed work with bounded waiting and recoverable unknowns, not the number of tasks accepted into memory.

This model does not specify an executor implementation or claim a runtime test. The inherited JDK references explain the execution context; the queue arithmetic and failure schedule here are original synthetic reasoning.

pages.editorial_addition:
## A four-window consumer recovery trace

In an original fictional booking consumer, an incoming message carries a stable logical identity. The consumer's local transaction attempts to record that identity and change the authoritative booking state. The two writes belong to the same commit boundary; a separate acknowledgment to the broker follows the durable outcome.

There are four different crash windows. Before either write commits, retry must be able to attempt the operation. After an identity is recorded but before the business effect commits, a design using separate transactions can falsely suppress a missing effect. After the business effect commits but before the identity commits, the inverse design can apply the effect twice. When both records commit together but the acknowledgment is lost, redelivery should recognize the already recorded result.

Concurrent delivery adds a separate race. Two handlers checking for absence before either commits can both believe the message is new. A uniqueness or equivalent atomic authority rule must decide which transaction can record the identity, with failure handled as part of the intended protocol rather than as an unrelated unexpected error.

This boundary covers effects controlled by that transaction. It cannot include an independently committed email or remote API call merely because the local handler invokes it. That second boundary needs its own durable intent, idempotency or reconciliation contract. The [original idempotent-consumer pattern](https://microservices.io/patterns/communication-style/idempotent-consumer.html) supplies the bounded recording pattern; this crash schedule is original reasoning and was not executed.

pages.title: MVCC snapshots and the lifetime of row versions
pages.question: Why can an old row version remain necessary after an update commits, and how does that differ from WAL durability?
pages.decision: Fill an actual explanatory gap: the original primary WAL manuscript names MVCC in the chapter title without giving snapshot/version-lifetime ownership its own explanation.
pages.editorial_addition:
## Visibility is a question about a reader

[PostgreSQL 17 section 13.1](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/17/mvcc-intro.html) describes a multiversion model in which statements observe a snapshot. A committed update therefore does not mean every concurrent reader must immediately interpret the new row version as its own view. Snapshot visibility and durable logging answer different questions: what this reader may observe, versus which changes can be recovered after a crash.

The useful architectural consequence is to identify the reader's observation boundary before describing a result as current. A dashboard query, a long-running report and a transaction enforcing an invariant can require different evidence. Avoid turning the existence of MVCC into a claim that no operation waits for a lock; explicit locks and write conflicts still belong to their own contracts.

## Isolation determines how the view evolves

[Section 13.2](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/17/transaction-iso.html) distinguishes Read Committed statement snapshots from Repeatable Read transaction snapshots. Successive statements at Read Committed can see concurrent committed changes. Repeatable Read retains a stable transaction view but does not itself exclude every serialization anomaly. Serializable transactions add a stronger committed-history guarantee and still require an application retry protocol when a transaction cannot commit.

Consider an original fictional report that reads an item classification, then reads its associated allocations. Another transaction commits between those statements. Decide whether the report permits that mixed observation before choosing isolation or application reconciliation. A stable snapshot can solve an observation problem without proving that two concurrent writers preserve the allocation invariant. The adjacent relational-isolation chapter owns that enforcement question.

## Old versions consume a lifecycle budget

[Section 24.1](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/17/routine-vacuuming.html) explains why updated or deleted versions cannot be removed while another transaction may still need to see them. Vacuuming can make obsolete-version space reusable after it is no longer needed. Ordinary reuse inside a relation is different from immediately shrinking its file on the operating system.

In an invented timeline, reader R begins before writer W commits a changed item. R may still need an earlier version under its snapshot, while a later reader can see the new one. Ending W is therefore not the same event as making every older version reclaimable. Keeping R open indefinitely can extend the relevant retention horizon; the magnitude and operational impact require actual observation, not a universal threshold.

| Question | Evidence needed | Invalid inference |
|---|---|---|
| What may R observe? | Isolation, snapshot and query contract | Latest committed data is automatically every reader's view |
| Can the old version be reused? | Visibility/retention horizon and maintenance progress | Writer commit alone proves the old version can disappear |
| Is a committed write recoverable? | WAL, storage and acknowledgment contract | Snapshot consistency proves crash durability |

## Failure probe and limits

A proposed experiment holds a read transaction open while another session updates the chosen rows. Record the reader's permitted observations, transaction lifetime and maintenance behavior, then end the reader and observe the later state. Do not change isolation, workload and maintenance configuration simultaneously and attribute every difference to one cause.

No PostgreSQL process was executed for this page. The official sections above were textually inspected; the report, row identities and schedule are original educational examples. They do not specify a production tuning value, a recovery objective or measured space growth. This page fills snapshot/version-lifetime explanation; WAL, replication and restore remain separate canonical questions.

## Original workload model — retained log is a recovery budget

Use a fictional change stream that generates ten units of log per second while an archival destination accepts six. During that interval the local archive backlog grows by four units per second. After thirty seconds the additional retained amount is 120 units, before considering any pre-existing backlog. Units are deliberately abstract: they are not bytes per transaction, a PostgreSQL measurement or a sizing recommendation.

If the destination later accepts fourteen units per second while generation remains ten, the backlog drains by four units per second. It therefore needs another thirty seconds to remove that additional backlog, assuming uninterrupted service and no other retention requirement. A healthy-looking average over the entire minute conceals the maximum amount that had to remain available locally.

The architecture question is what happens before that budget is exhausted. Identify which consumers or recovery objectives require the retained history, which failure can pause progress, who observes the backlog and what the permitted degraded action is. Deleting required history, refusing new work and adding storage have different correctness and availability consequences. Do not choose between them from a storage-utilization percentage alone.

The [PostgreSQL 17 WAL introduction](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/17/wal-intro.html) explains log-before-data ordering and recovery from logged changes. It does not establish this fictional generation rate, archive service rate or retention capacity. The arithmetic above is an illustrative queue model; real sizing additionally needs measured log generation, failure duration, recovery membership and the target deployment's actual retention rules.

## Original ranked-set counterexample — authorization is not optional relevance

Suppose an exact hypothetical ranking is A, B, C, D, E. The caller may read only D and E. A candidate stage that retrieves three items and then removes unauthorized results returns nothing. A search over the authorized population can return D and E. The difference follows from the declared sets; it is not an observed result for an ANN library or a promise about any engine's planner.

Increasing the candidate budget may help find authorized results in this example, but it must never change what is authorized. Conversely, filtering early is not enough to prove recall: the index, model and permitted population still define the search problem. Evaluate quality against an exact authorized reference, and record whether the candidate budget, filter selectivity or snapshot changed between runs.

Two negative cases matter. A revoked grant must prevent disclosure even when an old cached candidate list contains the document. An empty authorized result must not be reported as proof that the corpus contains no relevant document. The response can state that nothing was found in the permitted scope without revealing the existence or identity of excluded material.

These are original set-based examples, not a fresh pgvector or Faiss behavior claim. Product-specific execution order and index behavior remain governed by the inherited versioned sources and require compatible integration evidence before deployment.

## Original stale-edge counterexample

A later source revision S2 removes the call, but an independently rebuilt relationship store still serves the S1 edge. A query can traverse a syntactically valid path and nevertheless answer the wrong temporal question. The existence of an edge and successful query execution do not establish current source support.

Carry the inspected source identity, relation meaning and snapshot membership into any derived relationship. An update can mark a relationship stale or unknown instead of asserting that the absence of a new inspection proves removal. Conversely, deleting the stale edge must not silently erase the historical reason it once existed.

A useful negative experiment asks the same dependency question against S1, S2 and a mixed snapshot. Accept the historical answer only with S1 attribution; reject the mixed-snapshot conclusion or disclose the unresolved evidence. This is original conceptual reasoning. pages.editorial_addition:
## Original tabletop exercise — recovery must have an oracle

Prepare a fictional incident in which catalogue search is stale while the authoritative item store remains correct. Give participants a visible symptom, a current permission boundary and several plausible explanations. Do not give them a secret instruction to select a predetermined remedy. The exercise should reveal how they distinguish observations, hypotheses and authorized changes.

One person coordinates the response and assigns work; another owns a proposed operational action; a communication owner records what users currently experience. Before performing a hypothetical restart or traffic move, ask which invariant could be harmed, what evidence permits the action and what would trigger its reversal. An observer records when authority or ownership becomes ambiguous.

The success condition is not that participants eventually name the planted explanation. Require a bounded impact assessment, a durable decision chronology, a safe mitigation and an explicit check of user-visible correctness after mitigation. Include an action that restores process health without repairing stale state, so the team must distinguish a green deployment from a recovered service.

The [SRE Workbook incident-response chapter](https://sre.google/workbook/incident-response/) supports defining response roles, shared coordination and practice before an incident. The catalogue scenario, evaluation oracle and failure injection above are original educational proposals. No exercise was run and no recovery time was measured; a tabletop also does not demonstrate the target deployment's real failover or restore behavior.

## Original route acceptance matrix

Use paired questions that differ in a material input. One pair asks for a mechanism under a named version and then under an unavailable version. Another changes an ordinary caller into one without permission to inspect the candidate page. A third supplies a measured bottleneck and then removes the observation supporting that diagnosis. The expected route should change when the evidence changes.

For answerable cases, require the route to open the canonical mechanism, preserve its preconditions and cite the exact supporting passage. For unknown-version, denied-scope and missing-observation cases, require a bounded missing-evidence or refusal result. A relevant title alone must not make the case pass. Include a stale but plausible page to test whether the answer preserves snapshot identity.

Record the full reading path and the participating tool calls if this evaluation is later executed. A short final answer can still have an expensive or ungrounded route, so answer length is not the measurement of total work. The matrix is a proposed synthetic evaluation contract; no retrieval runtime or answer-quality benchmark was executed for this page.
